All 20 tech stocks on a list from financial newsletter The Kobeissi Letter trade at least 25% below record highs. CoreWeave (CRWV) leads the slide at 76%.

Additionally, the S&P 500 has lost over $6 trillion in six weeks adding pressure to the markets in general. The Nasdaq Composite, however, sits in correction territory, a 10% decline, not the 20% that defines a bear market.

Why Are Cloud and Chip Names Falling Hardest?

The deepest drops cluster in cloud computing, chips, and data storage. Oracle (ORCL) and SanDisk (SNDK), a flash memory maker, each trail their highs by 68%. Nebius (NBIS), an artificial intelligence (AI) cloud provider, is down 66%.

Intel (INTC) is down 61%. Western Digital (WDC), a data storage maker, and Arm (ARM), a chip designer, each trail by 60%. Tesla (TSLA) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) show the mildest declines at 25%, still beyond the 20% bear market line.

CoreWeave, which rents computing capacity to AI developers, grew third-quarter revenue 168% to $3.66 billion. Its net loss still reached $709 million, with net interest expense at $846 million, according to its results.

A correction means a 10% decline from a record, while a bear market requires 20%. The Nasdaq Composite closed at 23,879.20 on Nov. 19. That sits below the 24,315.00 close that confirmed its correction on Nov. 5, CNBC reported.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 fell 2.02% on Nov. 19 to 7,175.83. AMD fell further after short seller Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a bet against the chipmaker.

Will the Indexes Follow These Tech Stocks Lower?

The Kobeissi Letter, meanwhile, has described the selloff as a historic opportunity. In both earlier 2026 episodes, in March and July, the Composite later set new records, a Motley Fool analysis shows.

If that pattern holds, indexes could recover while these 20 stocks lag. A close 20% below the Oct. 6 record, however, would most likely break it.

His other trades involved Tencent, Adobe, Ero Copper and Temple & Webster.

'The Big Short' investor Michael Burry on Thursday disclosed several portfolio additions, beginning with Chinese electric-vehicle maker BYD, a direct Tesla competitor.

BYD At Multi-Year Lows

Burry said he added to his BYD holding (BYDDF). He noted the shares are at five-year lows and could fall further, but argued that most of the damage has already occurred. He highlighted that the U.S.-traded BYDDF represents actual shares of the Hong Kong-listed company, giving shareholders direct ownership.

"I believe long-term in BYD's competitive advantage against nearly all car companies," the investor said. BYD makes electrified vehicles, including both battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid vehicles. The company sold 4.6 million vehicles globally in 2025, including 4.5 million passenger vehicles, making it the world's largest EV seller.

Interestingly, Burry does not own shares of BYD's American rival Tesla. He shorted Tesla briefly in June but recovered that short for a gain in September. The investor has previously termed the stock "ridiculously overvalued" but noted that shorting it is "dangerous."

Other Chinese Holdings

Burry also bought more of Chinese e-commerce company JD.com's (JD) American depositary shares after an earnings-related pullback. Burry noted that JD has nearly $20 per ADS in cash and securities, is expected to earn $3 per share, and is trading in the $25s.

Separately, he added to Chinese technology conglomerate Tencent (TCEHY) on an earnings-related decline after remaining patient with the position. He called the current valuation "ridiculous," citing the company's dominant position in China and assets that cannot be replicated. Burry said he remains a believer even as AI-related spending has turned free cash flow negative, expressing trust in management.

Consumer, Mining And Software Adds

Burry increased exposure to U.S. grocery retailer Sprouts Farmers Market (SFM) through significantly out-of-the-money call options expiring in January 2028, citing cheap premiums, while acknowledging that the company faces a tough consumer dealing with inflation.

Trump Just Disclosed Tesla and SpaceX Stock Purchases. Here's What His Portfolio Moves Reveal
Jonathan Ponciano, The Motley Fool

President Donald Trump's latest stock transactions are out, and yes, Tesla and SpaceX made the list.

On Thursday, the Office of Government Ethics made public a 25-page transaction report covering hundreds of transactions from September. It shows purchases of Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) stock, along with sales of household names like McDonald's (NYSE:MCD) and Home Depot (NYSE:HD).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

So how have the moves panned out, and what do they say about the billionaire president's portfolio? So far, the results are mixed: Several of the stocks Trump sold have outperformed the Tesla and SpaceX shares he bought, and the filing seems to indicate a shift toward dividends and bonds rather than a big bet on Elon Musk.

The Tesla and SpaceX buys were small

Reports like this one list each trade as a dollar range rather than an exact amount. Trump's four Tesla purchases, made between Sept. 1 and Sept. 10, total between $117,004 and $330,000. His two SpaceX stock purchases add up to $16,002 to $65,000. He also bought $100,001 to $250,000 in SpaceX bonds that pay 5.35% interest and mature in 2031.

The president also had much bigger moves in the filing. On Sept. 23 alone, Trump sold shares of McDonald's, Home Depot, Comcast (NASDAQ:CMCSA) and Fidelity National Information Services (NYSE:FIS) worth $1,000,001 to $5 million apiece. He also sold Nike (NYSE:NKE) and Constellation Brands (NYSE:STZ) stock worth $500,001 to $1 million each. The single largest transaction in the report, made the same day, was a purchase of $5,000,001 to $25 million of the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (NYSEMKT:VIG).

The scorecard so far

Here's how each has done since the day of the transaction, based on that day's closing price and Thursday afternoon trading, according to Nasdaq data. The filing doesn't give the exact prices Trump paid or received.

The buys:

Tesla: up about 6% since Sept. 1, the day of its largest purchase

SpaceX: down about 7% since Sept. 24, the day of its largest purchase

Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF: up about 2% since Sept. 23

The Sept. 23 sales:

Constellation Brands: up 21%

McDonald's: up 14%

Home Depot: up 13%

Comcast: up 10%

Nike: down 5%

Fidelity National Information Services: down 25%

Four of the six big stocks Trump sold have climbed 10% or more since then. But the FIS sale dodged a 25% drop, marking the best call in the batch. In other words, it's a mixed record, like most investors', and of course, these are just short-term movements. Long-term the picture can look vastly different.

Key Takeaways

Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital opened a $680 million Tesla position in the third quarter, added to Meta Platforms and Micron, and sold out of Qualcomm and Applied Materials.

Tesla trades at about 180x forward earnings, and analysts' average target is just 7% above the price, so the new stake is a bet on Robotaxi profits that the estimates don't show yet.

Meta trades at about 19x forward earnings, below its own five-year average, and it's the move the numbers back best.

Qualcomm's falling estimates back that exit, while Applied Materials' estimates have risen even as its stock halved after Sept. 30.

Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital ended the third quarter with a brand-new stake in Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) and four fewer chip stocks, according to its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16. It also added to Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) and Micron (MU:NASDAQ), and sold out of Qualcomm (QCOM:NASDAQ) and Applied Materials (AMAT:NASDAQ), among others.

Tesla is the big new bet, and the priciest

Altimeter, which manages $18.75 billion in all, held $9.80 billion of US stocks in just 16 positions on Sept. 30. Tesla went straight to No. 4 on that list: 1.92 million shares worth $680 million, or 6.9% of its 13F stocks, in a stock Altimeter didn't own on June 30. Tesla is up 8% since Sept. 30, the only one of the quarter's three buys in the green.

That's a lot to pay, though. Tesla trades at about 180x forward earnings, well above its five-year quarter-end average of 112x. Its GAAP operating margin was 2.6% in the third quarter, down from 5.8% a year earlier, as R&D spending rose 69%. Tesla has guided 2026 capital spending to about $20 billion, more than double 2025's $8.5 billion, and analysts expect its free cash flow to stay negative through 2028. Anyone buying at this price is betting on Robotaxi, and CEO Elon Musk has said Robotaxi revenue should become noticeable by the second quarter of 2027.

More Meta, at a discount to its own history

Altimeter added 25% to Meta in the quarter, ending it with 1.70 million shares worth $1.23 billion. That's 12.6% of its 13F stocks and its second-largest position. The stock has fallen 15% since Sept. 30, but the business is still growing fast: third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion. At about 19x forward earnings, Meta trades below its five-year quarter-end average of 21x.

title: Trump's New Filing Reveals Nvidia, SpaceX And Tesla Purchases. White House Says He Didn't Direct Trades.

President Donald Trump's latest financial disclosure reveals purchases of Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla securities in September, placing some of the biggest names in American technology and defense among hundreds of transactions made while his administration was shaping policies affecting those industries.

The 25-page report released Thursday by the U.S. Office of Government Ethics lists 751 transactions, including investments in artificial intelligence companies, government contractors, exchange-traded funds and corporate bonds. It also documents major stock sales involving McDonald's, Home Depot and Comcast.

The disclosure raises questions about the potential overlap between the president's financial interests and decisions made by his administration, particularly as Washington considers restrictions on advanced AI chip exports and oversees billions of dollars in federal contracts involving companies such as SpaceX.

The White House maintains that Trump does not personally direct the transactions.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said third-party financial institutions independently manage the president's portfolio, following established investment indexes rather than instructions from Trump or his family.

"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," Ingle said in a statement to Reuters.

The filing, signed by Trump on Nov. 1 and received by the ethics office on Nov. 5, identifies several purchases of Nvidia stock during September. Reuters calculated that the transactions included up to $265,000 in purchases and up to $15,000 in sales.

The official disclosure reports transactions in broad dollar ranges rather than exact amounts, making it impossible to determine precisely how much the president paid for the shares or whether the investments generated profits.

The latest purchases follow much larger Nvidia transactions in August, when Trump reported buying as much as $1.6 million in shares and selling up to $1 million.

Nvidia is central to the administration's technology and trade policies because its advanced processors power many of the artificial intelligence systems being developed by American companies.

The United States has restricted exports of certain high-performance chips to China over national security concerns, while Nvidia executives have argued that access to the Chinese market is important for maintaining American technological leadership.

Musk made the remarks in Shenzhen during a meeting with Ren Hongbin, head of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, during APEC week. He described himself as a super fan of China.

The report gave no production target or timetable. Tesla's Shanghai plant builds the Model 3 and Model Y, has annual capacity of more than 950,000 vehicles and ships to markets including Europe, South Korea and Australia.

Shanghai wholesale sales reached 810,889 vehicles in the first 10 months of 2026, up 21.4% from a year earlier, according to China Passenger Car Association data compiled by CnEVPost.

Exports more than doubled to 420,984 vehicles over that period, while Chinese retail sales fell 15% to 389,905. In October alone, exports accounted for a record 87% of the factory's wholesale volume.

Investors Takeaway

The next monthly figures will help show where Tesla can sell the extra vehicles Musk wants Shanghai to build. If Chinese retail sales remain weak, overseas buyers will have to absorb more of the output.

The export and domestic sales breakdown will give investors a clearer read on demand than Shanghai's combined wholesale total alone.

Leverage has cut far deeper into the fund built to double Tesla's (NASDAQ:TSLA) daily moves than into the automaker's own stock in 2026. Direxion Daily TSLA Bull 2X ETF (NASDAQ:TSLL) shares are trading at $9.89 midday on Thursday, down 1.1%. The fund is down 50.46% year to date (YTD).

Tesla stock is at $381.45, down 16.11% YTD, and it's slipping alongside the fund. SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), the other public company tied to Tesla CEO Elon Musk, is trading at $140. SPCX shares are down 7% over the past month.

TSLA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

The bigger question for the Direxion fund is what it would take to get back to $20. It finished 2025 at $18.67 and last traded above $20 in August 2022, at $20.39.

How Daily Resets Turned Tesla's Slide Into a Deeper Loss

Direxion's fund seeks twice Tesla's return each day, then resets its leverage before the next session. Across weeks and months, each gain or loss compounds on a new base, so the fund's return can drift far from twice what Tesla delivered.

A return to $20 would need a strong, steady Tesla rally, and a volatile path could leave the fund behind even if Tesla stock ends higher.
